feed.title: Combined summary - Thoughts on a network policy for quantum-vulnerable UTXOs (long-exposure quantum attacks)

entry.title: Combined summary - Thoughts on a network policy for quantum-vulnerable UTXOs (long-exposure quantum attacks)
entry.summary: The emergence of quantum computing, particularly the anticipated event known as "Q-day," poses significant challenges to the security foundations of cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin. At its core, the concern centers on Unspent Transaction Outputs (UTXOs) that are vulnerable to quantum attacks, which could enable adversaries to break current cryptographic protections and steal funds. These vulnerabilities are primarily categorized into address type vulnerabilities—such as those in Pay to Public Key (P2PK) and Pay to Taproot (P2TR)—and address re-use vulnerabilities, each requiring distinct mitigation strategies. For address type vulnerabilities, proactive measures have been proposed to shield assets at risk. One approach involves freezing transactions from susceptible address types after Q-day, under the presumption that users would have had ample warning and time to migrate their funds to post-quantum secure addresses. This strict measure is based on the idea that any transaction from legacy types after Q-day is automatically suspect and potentially compromised. An alternative, more flexible strategy is to implement a rate-limit on spends from these vulnerable addresses, as seen in proposals like the "Hourglass." Such a mechanism aims to prevent market instability by avoiding mass liquidation of compromised coins, while also providing opportunities for legitimate owners to recover their assets through proof of ownership, potentially aided by white hat operators. Address re-use vulnerabilities present a more nuanced debate. Some view these as akin to user error, similar to generating insecure seed phrases, suggesting that affected UTXOs should remain spendable with no exceptional intervention. The rationale is that most funds at these addresses have already been used and that users are expected to relocate their assets to secure addresses before Q-day. Others advocate for a "cold sleep" or temporary freeze on these UTXOs, preventing immediate theft and allowing time to develop consensus-approved recovery processes, such as zero-knowledge proofs of seed phrase ownership. This method seeks to balance the urgent need to prevent catastrophic losses with the possibility of assisting those unable to move their funds in time. The timing and consensus for implementing these protective policies are crucial. Introducing freezes or rate-limits prematurely risks penalizing users who have yet to upgrade without exposing them to quantum attacks, while moving too late would fail to avert large-scale theft. Achieving network-wide agreement on when and how to enact these defenses remains a considerable challenge, highlighting the importance of timely decision-making and clear communication within the community. Technical proposals for adapting to the quantum threat include mechanisms like the Hourglass, which facilitates gradual access to funds that may otherwise be locked or frozen, thus minimizing disruptions for users who are temporarily unable to manage their assets. Post-Q-day, the handling of potentially stolen Bitcoin could mirror current practices for block rewards, with miners given discretion to prioritize transactions, especially those offering compensation. Additional safeguards, such as introducing a soft fork to require both traditional signatures and BIP39 proof for spending certain coins, are being considered to further tighten security, though this would predominantly affect very old coins whose movement is statistically unlikely. The broader philosophical question underlying these debates revolves around the core objective of Bitcoin: to enable individuals to secure and use their assets indefinitely, free from confiscation or theft. Quantum computing disrupts this promise for some legacy UTXOs, making it clear that there are limits to what technology alone can guarantee. Effective solutions will likely be partial mitigations rather than complete fixes, emphasizing the need for user education, timely upgrades, and adaptive protocols. As the landscape of cryptographic security evolves, so must the narrative surrounding Bitcoin’s immutability. The belief in unchangeable technological standards is no longer tenable; deliberate updates and human intervention are necessary to ensure ongoing resilience against emerging threats. For further insights and active discussions on managing quantum-vulnerable outputs—including ideas such as "active sweeping" after Q-day—additional resources can be explored at [delvingbitcoin.org](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/active-sweeping-of-vulnerable-outputs-after-q-day/2421).
